alt: Three look-alikes each missing something: a summary restates features with no claim, an opinion piece makes claims with no linguistic evidence, a list of theories describes research without applying it. Academic argument combines a claim that answers the question, linguistic evidence, applied research and awareness of other views.
caption: Argument needs a claim, evidence and other views together; each look-alike drops one.

alt: Seven components in order: a thesis in the introduction; claims as topic sentences; evidence from Section A data and studies; analysis of how it supports the claim; a counter-argument; evaluation of how far the claim holds; and a conclusion that answers directly.
caption: A thesis frames the essay; each paragraph claims, evidences, analyses and weighs; the conclusion refines.

alt: Six register tools with examples: hedging (“suggests”, “may indicate”), reporting verbs (“found” versus “claims”), impersonal constructions, precise terminology (“asymmetrical address” rather than “talking down”), cohesive discourse markers, and citation such as “(Labov, 1966)”.
caption: The writing itself is assessed: hedge, cite accurately and use precise terms.

after: ## Using Section A data as evidence
alt: A Section A observation (the in-group nickname “Captain” and a private abbreviation) becomes Section B evidence that in-group lexis marks the boundary of a group. Below, choose data that supports, complicates and, if possible, contradicts the thesis.
caption: Turn features into claims about language and groups, and use complicating data to evaluate.

alt: Studies grouped by theme. Social variation: Labov (1966) New York stores, Trudgill (1974) Norwich covert prestige, Milroy (1980) Belfast networks, Eckert (1989) jocks and burnouts. Interaction: Giles’s accommodation, Brown and Levinson (1987) politeness. Gender debate: Lakoff (1975), Tannen (1990) and Cameron (2007), from deficit to difference to critique of both.
caption: Know each finding accurately and use it to confirm, extend or challenge your own data.

alt: A five-part plan for the group-membership question using a football team’s chat: thesis that “mainly” overstates it; support from nicknames and banter (communities of practice, Eckert); complication from the captain’s imperatives (Wareing); counter from the coach’s formal register (accommodation); and a conclusion that the view is partly true but too narrow.
caption: Support, complicate, counter, then judge: the qualifying word drives the evaluation.
